initial_requirements: Computer users need a cross-platform graphical file and archive manager that brings multiple open-source compression utilities behind one consistent interface. Users should be able to create, update, extract, inspect, split, join, compare, and securely delete files or archives, apply checksums, and protect archives with credentials. Settings should accommodate different preferences, while both inexperienced and advanced users can access appropriate management capabilities.

slots.key: Confirmation and Impact Warning Rules

For secure delete, the product should explain the impact plainly and require an explicit warning that the data is being permanently removed before continuing. For overwriting or updating an archive in place, the confirmation should clearly state what will be replaced before the user continues. Changing permissions should also get a confirmation when it affects shared files or system locations, since it can block other users. Higher-risk cases should use a more specific, action-specific warning rather than a generic yes/no prompt. If an external archive command fails or produces output that cannot be verified, the product should say the operation failed and the result could not be verified in plain language, include archive/tool/error details if available, and make clear that no trusted completion was recorded. Before retry, overwrite, or deletion is allowed, the user should be offered to view the log or error details, keep the current files unchanged, or abandon the operation. If there is partial output, the product should ask whether to keep it for inspection or discard it, and must not do either automatically without warning. slots.key: Confirmation and impact-warning rules for high-risk actions
slots.value: Actions that can affect data loss, security, or other users’ work should have stronger, action-specific warnings than routine operations. For secure delete, overwriting, changing permissions, or updating an archive in place, the product should explain the impact plainly and ask for confirmation before continuing. Secure delete should always include an explicit warning that the data will be permanently removed. In-place archive updates or overwrites should clearly state what will be replaced before the user continues. Changing permissions should also require confirmation when it affects shared files or system locations, since it can block other users. The warning should be direct and action-specific rather than generic, so the user understands the consequence before proceeding. For novice users in the simple interface, the confirmation should use plain language that explains what will happen and what could be lost, not just the technical action name. For the highest-risk actions, an additional 'I understand' style checkbox is preferred. It should be blocked instead of allowed when the action would clearly cause irreversible loss, when the target is protected or system-managed, or when the product cannot verify that the user has permission. In those cases, a warning alone is not enough; the action should be prevented until the user uses a more advanced path or corrects the conditions.

slots.key: Update delivery and installation control
slots.value: Use a mixed approach: automatic update checks are helpful, but installation should be optional or controlled, especially for managed or locked-down systems. For business users and managed systems, update checks should be lightweight and run on launch or on an admin-controlled schedule rather than constantly in the background. In managed environments, the default check should be at launch time only, with an admin-set interval available for organizations that want periodic checks. A manual check should always be allowed if the user has permission, because that’s useful for support and troubleshooting. Checks should be suppressed entirely when the machine is offline by policy, during a maintenance freeze, or if the organization has explicitly disabled outbound update traffic. If the system is marked as locked down, even a silent check can be considered too much, so that needs to follow whatever the admin policy says. Installation should be blocked or require approval when the machine is policy-managed, the user lacks admin rights, or the update would change file associations, shell integration, or other system-wide settings. Automatic updates should be disabled entirely in tightly controlled environments such as kiosks, locked-down enterprise desktops, or offline systems; in those cases, only update notifications should be shown and deployment should be handled by IT or an approved user process.
